c: A slab of granodiorite about 112 centimeters tall, carrying one message in three scripts.
Soldiers of a French expedition dug it up in 1799, while rebuilding a fort in the Nile Delta.
Its decree, issued at Memphis in 196 BC, appears in hieroglyphic, Demotic, and Greek.
Champollion used it in 1822 to crack the hieroglyphs after fourteen centuries of silence.
It is the British Museum’s most visited object, and shorthand for the key to any puzzle.
w: Three scripts, one message: without it, Egypt’s written past stays sealed.

c: Ten kilos of gold, inlaid with lapis lazuli, quartz, and obsidian.
It was fashioned around 1323 BC for a king who died before his twentieth year.
Howard Carter’s crew opened its case in 1922 and saw “wonderful things” by candlelight.
The striped headdress bears a cobra and a vulture — the Two Ladies of Egypt.
The face of the boy king’s tomb, and of a whole lost dynasty.
w: The boy king was a footnote of history; the mask made him immortal.

c: Thirty-odd bronze gears, corroded and split, pulled from a Roman-era shipwreck in 1901.
Nothing else like it is known for the next fourteen centuries.
Its hand-cranked dials tracked the sun, the moon, and the planets through the zodiac.
It computed the Metonic cycle, predicted eclipses, and even marked the Olympiad games.
Often called the world’s first computer — a Greek astronomical machine from around 100 BC.
w: Someone built a planetarium in bronze a thousand years before clockwork existed anywhere else.

c: A shepherd chasing a stray goat threw a stone into a Judean cave and heard pottery break — so one account goes.
Eleven caves near Qumran gave up fragments of some 900 manuscripts between 1946 and 1956.
Most were written on parchment in Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek, some two thousand years ago.
They include the oldest known copies of the Hebrew Bible, a millennium older than anything before them.
Today most of them rest in the Shrine of the Book in Jerusalem.
w: Every modern Bible translation leans, at some verse, on a cave near the Dead Sea.

c: Parian marble, about two meters tall, missing both arms — the holes for her bracelets survive.
A farmer unearthed her in 1820 on the Aegean island of Melos.
She was carved around 100 BC, a blend of Classical ideals and Hellenistic drama.
She may have held an apple — melos means apple — or a shield, or a spindle.
The Louvre’s armless goddess, sold to France within months of her discovery.
w: Two arms are missing; the argument about them never ends.

c: Local well-diggers near Xi’an struck a head of hardened clay in 1974.
An estimated 8,000 soldiers stand in the ranks — and no two faces are alike.
They were painted in bright lacquers that flaked within minutes of excavation.
Each carries real bronze weapons, some still sharp after 2,200 years.
They guard the tomb of Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor of China.
w: One emperor, one afterlife army — bureaucracy rendered in clay.

c: Iron plates, tinned bronze, and garnets — smashed into some 500 pieces and buried in a ship.
It was dug from an East Anglian mound in 1939, on the eve of war.
The face-mask has eyebrows ending in gilded boars, and a dragon flies across the crest.
The 27-meter ship beneath the mound rotted away, leaving only its ghost pressed in sand.
The crowning find of Anglo-Saxon England, probably the grave-goods of King Raedwald.
w: An entire ship dissolved to a shadow in the sand; the helmet refused.

c: Not a tapestry at all: seventy meters of embroidered wool on linen.
Its Latin captions run from 1064 to 1066 and stop mid-scene.
A famous comet streaks across one sky, above frightened courtiers.
It ends with the fall of the housecarls on the ridge near Hastings.
The Normans’ own picture-book of the conquest of England.
w: The winners embroidered their version, and it outlasted every chronicle.

c: Ninety-three pieces of walrus ivory and whale tooth, found in a sand dune in 1831.
Most now sit in the British Museum; Edinburgh holds the rest.
The queens rest their cheeks on their hands; the berserkers bite their shields.
They were carved in Norway around 1150, likely for trade to the Norse isles.
The most famous chess set of the Middle Ages — from the Isle of Lewis in the Hebrides.
w: Vikings played the same endgames we do.

c: A painted limestone core under a coat of stucco, about 47 centimeters tall.
One eye was never finished — a teaching piece, or something stranger.
Ludwig Borchardt’s expedition dug her from a sculptor’s studio at Amarna in 1912.
Her name means “the beautiful one has come,” and her blue crown is like no other queen’s.
She has watched over Berlin for a century, while Egypt keeps asking her home.
w: A portrait so perfect it became a diplomatic problem.

c: Two German hikers found a body melting out of a glacier in 1991 — and assumed it was a modern death.
He carried 61 tattoos, an axe of nearly pure copper, and shoes of bearskin and deer hide.
His last meals were ibex and red deer, einkorn bread, and bracken — his final day was busy.
An arrowhead in his left shoulder, and traces of four others’ blood on his blade, told of a violent end.
Europe’s oldest natural human mummy, 5,300 years old, now rests in Bolzano, Italy.
w: Five thousand years later, we know what he ate for breakfast — and who he fought at the end.

c: A poplar panel, 77 by 53 centimeters — smaller than most hardcover books.
It was never delivered: the artist carried it from Florence toward France, adjusting it for years.
The sitter was Lisa Gherardini, wife of a silk merchant.
In 1911 a handyman walked out of the Louvre with it under his smock; Picasso was briefly a suspect.
Leonardo’s portrait with the famous smile — the most visited painting on earth.
w: The most famous smile in the world was a commission portrait.

c: A canvas painted from memory, looking east before sunrise through a barred window.
The village below is invented; the cypress in the foreground is real.
It was painted in June 1889, from a quiet asylum at Saint-Rémy-de-Provence.
Eleven stars and a wavy moon swirl above a landscape the artist never saw so calmly again.
Van Gogh’s swirling night over Provence — an icon of the Museum of Modern Art since 1941.
w: Painted from an asylum window, and brighter than anything in the sky outside it.

c: A bull, a horse, a light bulb shaped like an eye, a weeping mother — all in black, white, and grey.
It was painted in about three weeks of fury in a Paris studio, in May 1937.
A tapestry copy hangs at the United Nations, where world leaders file past it.
It answered a market town bombed on a Monday, by planes of the Condor Legion.
Picasso’s enormous anti-war painting of a Basque town’s destruction, now at the Reina Sofía.
w: Commissioned for a pavilion, it grew too large for any war but the one it showed.

c: Cast twice, because the first one cracked on its first test ring.
It carries a line from Leviticus: “Proclaim liberty throughout all the land.”
The famous crack grew through decades of ringing, until 1846.
It rang — or so the story goes — for the first public reading of the Declaration of Independence.
Philadelphia’s cracked bell, moved indoors from Independence Hall in 1976.
w: A bell too cracked to ring, and impossible to retire.

c: Spruce and muslin, a twelve-horsepower engine, and a landing gear of skids.
It cost about a thousand dollars and had no wheels — it launched from a rail.
Its longest flight on the first day lasted 59 seconds, into a cold December wind.
The pilot lay prone beside the engine; roll control came from warping the wingtips.
The 1903 Kitty Hawk machine — the first powered airplane, now hanging at the Smithsonian.
w: Twelve horsepower and twelve seconds of flight, and the century turned over.

c: A cone of steel and honeycomb: three couches, five windows, and a heat shield.
While two men walked on the Moon, its pilot photographed the landing site and waited alone for 21 hours.
It splashed down in the Pacific southwest of Hawaii on July 24, 1969, and went straight to quarantine.
Its name was picked at nearly the last minute — after the island of the Statue of Liberty.
Columbia, the command module of Apollo 11, now rests in Washington, D.C.
w: One astronaut kept the ship while the whole world looked at the Moon.

c: A black diorite pillar, 2.25 meters tall, carved with about 4,000 lines of cuneiform.
It was carted off to Susa as war booty around 1150 BC, and dug up again in 1901.
Its prologue says the gods called a king “to cause justice to prevail in the world.”
Law 196 is famous, and grim: an eye for an eye.
Hammurabi’s law code of Babylon, from around 1754 BC — in the Louvre.
w: Justice so old it carved the punishments into stone where nobody could soften them.

c: Sixty-four bronze guns, two decks, and a stern covered in painted lions and Greek heroes.
It sailed about 1,300 meters on its maiden voyage — then heeled, flooded, and sank.
The 1628 disaster killed around thirty people; the inquest blamed nobody by name.
It sat in Stockholm harbor for 333 years, until a wreck-hunter raised it in 1961, nearly intact.
Sweden’s top-heavy royal warship, now the centerpiece of its own museum.
w: A ship that sank in front of half of Stockholm, then waited for them to come back.

c: A 45.5-carat blue stone whose legend keeps accumulating deaths it never caused.
It was cut from the “French Blue,” stolen from the Crown Jewels in 1792.
It glows red under ultraviolet light, phosphorescing for minutes after the lamp goes off.
Its owners’ misfortunes — the newspapers said — ran from a beheaded queen to a sunk liner; the records mostly say otherwise.
The deep-blue diamond mailed to the Smithsonian in a plain brown wrapper, in 1958.
w: A rock with better publicists than geologists.

c: A giant block of Carrara marble, abandoned for decades after two sculptors botched it.
It stands 5.17 meters, its head and right hand enlarged on purpose — for the view from below.
The sling is over the shoulder and the stone hides in the left hand: ambush, not duel.
It took its place outside the Palazzo Vecchio in Florence in 1504, a symbol of the republic.
Michelangelo’s shepherd-giant, now in the Accademia gallery.
w: A block two sculptors ruined, and a 26-year-old who saw the shepherd inside.

c: A single sheet of calfskin, close to A4, in abbreviated Latin — sealed, not signed.
It was annulled by the Pope within ten weeks of Runnymede.
A third of its 63 clauses are about forests; only a few lines of it remain in law today.
“No free man shall be taken or imprisoned...” — clause 39, a seed of due process.
King John’s 1215 Great Charter, the grandfather of constitutional law.
w: A peace treaty that failed in ten weeks and outlived every king who signed it.

c: Nearly a thousand of them, most with bodies buried, ring a remote Pacific island.
They stand with their backs to the sea, eyes once inlaid with coral and obsidian.
The heaviest moved weighs over 80 tons, by a method still argued over — walked upright, some say.
They were carved from a single quarry at Rano Raraku between about 1250 and 1500.
The stone heads of Rapa Nui — Easter Island.
w: Faces for the ancestors, carved until the island ran out of trees to move them.

c: A gravel pit in Sussex gave up skull fragments and a jaw in 1912: England’s first “early man.”
The jaw was stained, the teeth filed flat — quiet doubts simmered for four decades.
He solved an awkward problem: why had England no early humans when France and Germany had plenty?
Fluorine dating raised the flag in 1949; by 1953 he was exposed as a patchwork fake.
The most famous scientific forgery of the century: a medieval human skull and an ape’s jaw.
w: England wanted an ancestor, so somebody arranged one.

c: No single author: a Mainz goldsmith in debt squeezed out about 180 copies in the 1450s, and some 49 survive.
Its two volumes hold 42 lines of type to the page, inked by a press rather than a scribexe2x80x99s hand.
Copies on paper and on vellum were finished by hand, the red headings brushed in after the press was done.
The first major book of the Western printing revolution, it broke the scriptoriaxe2x80x99s thousand-year monopoly.
It carries the name of Johannes Gutenberg, whose workshop launched the age of the printed page.
w: Before it, a book took a scribe a season; after it, a press could make hundreds. Reading, and history itself, never moved the same way again.

c: A barrel of baked clay about 23 centimeters long, covered in cramped little wedges.
The wedges are Babylonian cuneiform, composed in the style of that cityxe2x80x99s own royal inscriptions.
It celebrates a conquest won without a battle: Babylon fell to a Persian king in October 539 BCE.
The new ruler let deported peoples go home, which is why one biblical book remembers him kindly.
Written for Cyrus the Great, dug from Babylonxe2x80x99s ruins in 1879, it now keeps quiet in the British Museum.
w: Conquest, propaganda, and a kinder empire than most: an imperial press release in clay, from 539 BCE.

c: A gold funeral face about 30 centimeters tall, beaten from a single sheet with chased detail.
In 1876 it came out of a shaft grave at Mycenae, dug by a German businessman with a gift for timing.
The eyes are slit shut, the mouth is calm, and the hair is braided into rows of tiny curls.
The finder reportedly wired his king that he had gazed upon the face of Agamemnon, and the name never came off.
It is centuries older than the Trojan War of Homer, and whispers of tampering have followed it since the day it surfaced.
w: Schliemannxe2x80x99s timing was perfect and his names were not: the mask is royal, Mycenaean, and about 3,500 years old, but Agamemnon it is not.

c: Four gospels in 340 leaves, made by monks around 800 CE, probably begun on Iona and finished at Kells in Ireland.
Whole pages are surrendered to ornament: animals, knots, and tangled letters teem in colors ground from distant ores.
Viking raids scattered the community that began it, and in 1007 a thief stole its greatest volume from the abbey church for its golden cover.
The book came back within months, its cover gone, and it has been a celebrity of Irish Christianity ever since.
It has lived in the library of Trinity College Dublin since the 1660s, where visitors queue past its open pages.
w: Irelandxe2x80x99s monks called it the great relic of Columba. Call it the most extravagantly decorated book that survives, and few will argue.

c: A two-layer Roman glass: cobalt blue beneath a crust of white, cut away like a cameo to leave figures afloat.
It was made about two thousand years ago, and the scene, gods or lovers or both, has never been settled.
By tradition it was found in an ancient marble coffin near Rome and passed through the palaces of cardinals.
In 1845 a visitor hurled a nearby object at it in the British Museum and smashed it to pieces; it was restored from the shards.
Its name comes from a duke of Portland, and it has stood in the British Museum since 1810.
w: Two millennia of survival, undone in seconds by one man on a spree, then reassembled from a basket of shards.

c: A racing board of twenty squares, its wood inlaid with shell, red limestone, and lapis lazuli.
Players threw tetrahedral dice and raced pieces home, landing on rosette squares for an extra throw.
It was buried in the royal cemetery of Ur around 2600 BCE, among the tombs Leonard Woolley opened in the 1920s.
Its rules survived on a Babylonian clay tablet, decoded in the 1980s by the British Museumxe2x80x99s Irving Finkel.
One of the boards lives in London and a sister in Philadelphia, and both are still perfectly playable.
w: The oldest board game we can still play by its own written rules: five thousand years old, and backgammon is its descendant.

c: A guardian with a bullxe2x80x99s body, eaglexe2x80x99s wings, and a crowned manxe2x80x99s face, worked in five legs.
From the front it stands still; from the side it strides. The fifth leg makes both true at once.
Between its legs, cuneiform credits Ashurnasirpal II with the palace gate it held in the ninth century BCE.
Four meters of gypsum, weighing tonnes, it guarded Nimrud for an Assyrian king who called himself king of the world.
The ones that stayed in Iraq were sledgehammered by ISIS in 2015; the others stand guard in London, Paris, and Chicago.
w: An empirexe2x80x99s doorman, three thousand years on the job, now guarding museum halls instead of kings.

c: A disc of fired clay about 15 centimeters across, stamped on both faces with 241 crisp marks.
The 45 different signs run in a spiral from rim to center, pressed with ready-made seals rather than written by hand.
A Cretan palace gave it up in 1908, in a layer that dates it near 1700 BCE.
Because every mark was stamped, some call it the oldest printed text on Earth, and it certainly is the strangest.
Dozens of scholars have claimed to read it in as many languages, and none of the claims has convinced the others.
w: The worldxe2x80x99s most famous unreadable sentence: 45 stamps, one spiral, and thirty-seven centuries of silence.

c: In July 2009 a metal detectorist in a Midlands field heard a signal and started digging into gold.
Out came more than four thousand pieces, nearly all war gear: sword fittings, helmet fragments, and biblical scenes in gold and garnet.
There was not a single coin in the hoard, which is one of its genuine mysteries.
It went into the ground around 650 CE, in the age of Merciaxe2x80x99s warrior kings, and nobody ever came back for it.
The find was valued at 3.28 million pounds, split between finder and landowner, and raised by public appeal in a matter of weeks.
w: Four kilograms of warrior gold, hidden in a field for thirteen centuries, and not a word anywhere about why.

c: Eleven centimeters of limestone, carved while the Ice Age held Europe, about 30,000 years ago.
Heavy hips, folded arms, and braid upon braid of hair, all worked with care, and a face left entirely blank.
Traces of red ochre still ride her surface, the meaning of which went unrecorded.
She was dug from a terrace above the Danube in 1908, near the Austrian village of Willendorf.
She keeps house in Viennaxe2x80x99s Natural History Museum, and the stone she is cut from glitters with tiny fossils.
w: Older than farming, older than writing, older than every king in this puzzle: somebodyxe2x80x99s hands made her, and she remains.
